sounds.intro: Danish is written in the Latin alphabet with three extra letters at the end: æ, ø, å. Nouns are "en" or "et" words. Danish is famous for soft consonants and for swallowed word endings, so listen a lot.
rows: say "ur" with rounded lips, like "ur" in "fur"
say "ee" with rounded lips, like German "ü"
a rounded "oo", with the lips forward
a soft "th" as in "the", between vowels and at the end of words
made at the back of the throat, and it often sounds like a vowel
often fades into a "w" or "i" sound
a catch in the throat on some words, like a short "uh-oh"
at the end of a word, like "ee"
notes: Double consonants make the vowel before them short. A single consonant after a stressed vowel means the vowel is long.
Many Danish words are pronounced very differently from how they are spelt. Learn the sound of each word, not just the spelling.

grammar.title: Pronouns
text: Danish always uses the pronoun. "Du" is you. "Han" is he, "hun" is she, "det" or "den" is it. The polite "De" is old-fashioned.

grammar.title: Singular and plural
text: Nouns are "en" or "et" words. Plurals end in -er, -e, or have no ending. Learn the plural with each noun.

grammar.title: To be: være
text: "At være" (to be) has one form for everyone in the present: er.

grammar.title: Have: have
text: "At have" (to have) is "har" in the present for everyone. "Der er" means "there is".

grammar.title: Present tense
text: Add -r or -er to the stem. At arbejde (to work): jeg arbejder. The ending is the same for every person.

grammar.title: Basic sentences
text: The verb is always the second item: Jeg læser en bog. If another word comes first, the verb still stays second: I dag læser jeg en bog.

grammar.title: Negation
text: Put "ikke" after the verb: Jeg går ikke. In questions and with a second verb, "ikke" comes after the subject.
ex: I do not have a car
he does not work on Sundays

grammar.title: Asking questions
text: Put the verb first: Er du elev? A question word goes before the verb: Hvor bor du?

grammar.title: Question words
text: A question word comes first, then the verb.

grammar.title: Possessives and liking
text: The word agrees with the noun: min / mit / mine (my), din / dit / dine (your), hans, hendes, vores (our), jeres (your, plural), deres (their). To like something, use "at kunne lide".

grammar.title: Formal vs informal
text: Danish almost always uses "du", even with strangers and older people. "De" is old-fashioned and sounds stiff. Use "du".
ex: vær så venlig at sætte Dem
vair soh VEN-lee at SET-uh dem

grammar.title: Past and future (simple)
text: Past: add -ede, -te, or a changed stem. Jeg arbejdede (I worked), jeg gik (I went). Future: "skal", "vil" or "kommer til at" + verb.

grammar.title: Commands
text: Use the bare stem: kom. Add "vær så venlig" to be polite. To forbid, use "ikke".

grammar.title: Can, must, want
text: Kunne (can): jeg kan. Skulle or måtte (must): jeg skal, jeg må. Ville (want): jeg vil. The second verb stays in its basic form.
ex: I do not want to eat

grammar.title: In, on, at
text: Common words: i (in), på (on, at), ved (at, by), til (to), fra (from), med (with), under (under).
ex: the book is on the table
the cat is under the table
the shop is next to the bank
butikken ligger ved siden af banken
boo-TIK-en LIG-er veh SEE-dhen a BAN-ken
the park is near the station
the key is in the bag

grammar.title: Comparing things
text: Add -ere for "more", -est for "the most": hurtig, hurtigere, hurtigst. Some are irregular: stor, større, størst. "Than" is "end".
ex: det her er bedre end det der
deh hair air BEDH-ruh en deh dair
det her er værre end det der
deh hair air VAIR-uh en deh dair

grammar.title: Everyday sentences
text: Quick sentences to copy and change.
ex: vær så venlig at sætte Dem
vair soh VEN-lee at SET-uh dem
